title: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari
author: Robin Sharma
short_description: Robin Sharma’s fable of waking up — simplify, practice daily disciplines, and trade status for a richer inner life.
content_text:
PART 1 — KEY LESSONS (OUTLINE)

1. A collapse can become a curriculum

  • Julian Mantle’s courtroom heart attack is not only a medical emergency; it is a signal that a life built on status, speed, and applause can hollow out the person winning the race. Crisis becomes useful when it forces an honest inventory of what you traded for success.

2. Outer trophies do not guarantee inner peace

  • Wealth, a Ferrari, and courtroom dominance can coexist with exhaustion, emptiness, and fear. Sharma’s fable argues that fulfillment requires an inner operating system, not a bigger collection of symbols.

3. The mind is a garden you either tend or abandon

  • Thoughts grow into attitudes, then into character and destiny. Guard attention, plant useful ideas, and weed worry before it becomes the landscape of your days.

4. Purpose is a lighthouse, not a mood

  • Without a clear aim, busyness masquerades as meaning. A defined purpose organizes choices, energy, and courage the way a lighthouse organizes a ship’s course in fog.

5. Kaizen and discipline turn intention into identity

  • Daily incremental improvement and trained willpower matter more than dramatic overhauls. Small kept promises build the pink cable of self-control that carries larger ambitions.

6. Time and presence are the real currency

  • Respecting hours, designing rituals, and living in the present moment protect joy from being postponed until “someday after the next win.”

7. Service and simplicity complete the path

  • Contribution to others and shedding success theater — status performance for its own sake — convert personal growth into a life that feels light, useful, and awake.

PART 2 — THE MONK WHO SOLD HIS FERRARI

A 28-Minute Read Summary

Chapter 1: The wake-up call

Robin Sharma opens with a portrait of Julian Mantle at the peak of a certain kind of Western triumph. He is a brilliant trial lawyer, famous for ferocious preparation and courtroom theater. He owns the symbols that announce arrival: a gleaming red Ferrari, a mansion, tailored suits, and a calendar stuffed with high-stakes cases. Colleagues envy the package. What they cannot see as clearly is the cost. Julian sleeps poorly, eats poorly, and treats his body like a machine that will somehow keep producing under unlimited load. His mind races from one adversarial contest to the next. Pleasure is intermittent and shallow. Even victories taste brief because the next battle is already waiting.

The wake-up arrives without metaphor. In the middle of a heated trial, Julian collapses. A heart attack cuts through the performance. The public drama of the courtroom becomes a private reckoning in a hospital bed. Sharma uses this event to ask a blunt question many high achievers avoid: if you win every external contest and lose your health, relationships, and sense of meaning, what exactly did you win? The Ferrari still exists. The reputation still exists. But the person who earned them can no longer pretend the system is sustainable.

What follows is not a lecture on quitting ambition. It is a confrontation with unbalanced ambition. Julian’s life had one scoreboard: status, money, and professional dominance. Missing from that scoreboard were stillness, vitality, friendship beyond networking, and a purpose larger than the next verdict. The heart attack does not automatically make him wise. It makes him unable to keep lying to himself. That honesty is the first asset of transformation.

Sharma also plants a quieter character, John, a younger lawyer who admired Julian’s fire and feared his unraveling. John becomes the reader’s stand-in. He is competent, ambitious, and already showing early signs of the same bargain: trade presence for promotion, trade health for hustle, trade wonder for winning. The wake-up call is therefore double. Julian receives a medical crisis. John receives a living warning. Readers receive both.

After recovery, Julian does something that shocks his peers. He sells the mansion and the Ferrari, leaves the firm, and disappears. Rumors fill the vacuum. Some say he cracked. Some say he fled. Sharma’s point is sharper: Julian finally treated his life as something he could redesign rather than merely endure. The wake-up call matters only if it produces a new curriculum. Otherwise it becomes another story you tell at dinner about how busy and important you once were.

Lesson: Treat physical or emotional collapse as feedback that your success system is incomplete, then redesign the life that produced the crash.

Chapter 2: A fable of transformation

Years later, Julian returns looking almost unrecognizable: calm, radiant, lean, and oddly youthful. He finds John and begins to tell the story of where he went and what he learned. The narrative shifts into fable mode. Julian traveled to India seeking wisdom, eventually reaching a mythical Himalayan community of sages in Sivana. There he meets Yogi Raman and a circle of monks who live simply, train rigorously, and treat character as a craft. The setting is deliberately storybook. Sharma is not writing a travel documentary; he is building a teaching vehicle.

In Sivana, Julian learns that the sages preserve their philosophy through a symbolic story — a memorable mental movie rather than a dry list of rules. The movie contains seven images that encode seven virtues of an enlightened life. A magnificent garden represents the mind. A towering lighthouse represents purpose. A sumo wrestler represents kaizen, the practice of continuous self-improvement. A pink wire cable wrapped around the wrestler represents discipline and willpower. A golden stopwatch represents respect for time. Roses represent selfless service and kindness. A path of diamonds represents living fully in the present. Each image is vivid so the lesson can survive busyness and forgetfulness.

This chapter matters because it reframes self-help as apprenticeship. Julian does not become peaceful by reading a slogan. He submits to a way of life: early rising, contemplation, physical training, study, silence, and service. Transformation is shown as embodied practice inside a culture that normalizes depth. When he returns to the West, he does not bring souvenirs; he brings a portable curriculum. The fable becomes a bridge between monastery clarity and modern complexity.

John listens with a mixture of skepticism and hunger. That tension is useful. Many readers recognize themselves in both men: the part that wants proof, and the part that already knows the old life is too noisy. Sharma’s method is Socratic storytelling. Julian does not demand belief; he invites experiment. Try the practices. Watch what changes in sleep, focus, patience, and joy. Let results argue.

The deeper claim of the fable is that wisdom traditions and high-performance living need not be enemies. Julian once believed that intensity required agitation. The monks show him a different intensity: deliberate, serene, and sustained. He learns that calm is not the opposite of excellence; it is often the platform for it. Selling the Ferrari is symbolic subtraction — releasing the identity of “I am what I display” so a sturdier identity can form: “I am what I practice.”

Lesson: Use a vivid inner story and daily apprenticeship, not more trophies, as the engine of lasting personal change.

Chapter 3: Master your mind

The first virtue begins in the garden. Yogi Raman teaches that the mind is like soil: neglect it and weeds of worry, comparison, and fear take over; tend it and you grow clarity, courage, and creativity. Julian had treated his mind as a courtroom weapon aimed outward, never as a garden requiring daily care. The result was mental clutter so dense that even success felt like pressure. Mastery of life, in this framework, starts with mastery of attention.

Practical mind-mastery in the book includes several interlocking disciplines. One is guarding the gate of perception — being careful about the conversations, media, and environments that plant seeds. Another is concentration training: learning to hold attention on a single object, breath, or task long enough that the mind becomes a servant rather than a tyrant. Another is visualization: deliberately rehearsing the character and outcomes you intend to live, so imagination serves growth instead of anxiety. Sharma’s monks treat thoughts as causes, not mere commentary. What you repeatedly think, you eventually become inclined to do.

Julian also learns the Heart of the Rose practice: sitting quietly with a rose, studying its detail, and returning attention whenever it wanders. The rose is not mystical decoration; it is a concentration gym. Modern readers can translate the tool without needing a monastery. Choose one object of focus — breath, a candle, a paragraph of reading — and train the return. The skill that matters is not never drifting; it is noticing drift and coming back without drama.

Opposition thinking appears as another mental tool: when a negative interpretation arises, deliberately generate a more constructive and equally plausible framing. This is not denial. It is refusing to let the first fearful story become the only story. If a setback appears, ask what skill it is demanding. If criticism appears, ask what signal is useful and what ego is amplifying. The garden metaphor insists on active gardening. Passive minds are not neutral; they are overgrown.

Mastering the mind also means reducing the inner civil war. Julian’s old life ran on adrenaline and argument. The new training values serenity as a performance advantage. A calm mind notices opportunities a frantic mind misses. A calm mind recovers faster after conflict. A calm mind can choose a response instead of launching a reaction. In that sense, mental mastery is not soft; it is strategic.

Lesson: Tend your attention daily — concentrate, visualize wisely, and weed toxic thoughts — because your mind-garden becomes your life.

Chapter 4: Follow your purpose

The lighthouse virtue answers a different failure mode: a life that is busy but aimless. The monks teach that purpose is the organizing light that keeps a person from crashing into reefs of distraction. Julian’s earlier purpose was mostly comparative and external — win more, earn more, be seen as the best. That kind of purpose can motivate for years and still leave a person empty, because it never asks what the victory is for.

Sharma’s treatment of purpose is practical rather than purely poetic. Purpose should be written, revisited, and used as a filter for decisions. When you know the contribution you want your life to make, calendars become easier to edit. Opportunities that once looked shiny become obvious detours. Courage rises because hardship is interpreted as tuition toward a meaningful aim rather than random suffering. The lighthouse does not remove storms; it gives navigation during them.

Julian learns to craft a personal mission statement — a short declaration of who he intends to be and what he intends to give. The statement is not corporate branding for the self. It is a compass kept close enough to influence morning choices. Without it, motivation becomes weather. With it, motivation becomes a renewable resource tied to identity and service.

Purpose also protects against the trap of borrowed dreams. Many people chase goals installed by parents, peers, or industry culture. The fable pushes for an examined aim: What would make your days feel useful even if applause were removed? What strengths do you feel responsible to develop? Whom do you feel called to help? These questions sound soft until you notice how many hard-driving professionals cannot answer them without listing titles.

Importantly, purpose in this book is paired with action. A lighthouse that no sailor heeds is decoration. Once purpose is clear, the remaining virtues become methods for living it: mind training to stay clear, kaizen to improve capacity, discipline to follow through, time respect to protect the work, service to keep the aim generous, and presence to enjoy the voyage rather than postponing life until arrival.

Lesson: Write a living purpose that filters your choices, so ambition serves meaning instead of replacing it.

Chapter 5: Practice kaizen daily

The sumo wrestler in the fable stands for kaizen — continuous, incremental self-improvement. The image is intentionally odd and memorable: a giant wrestler embodying the philosophy of tiny daily gains. Julian learns that transformation fails when people demand overnight reinvention and then quit when reality refuses the fantasy. The Sivana method prefers steady pressure applied to mind, body, and character every day.

Kaizen here covers multiple domains. Physically, train the body so energy supports consciousness; a neglected body makes a cloudy mind. Mentally, stretch learning: read, study, reflect, and expand skills beyond the minimum required by your job. Spiritually or ethically, improve the quality of your motives — less ego theater, more sincerity. The point is whole-person upgrading. Specializing in career advancement while decaying everywhere else is the pattern that broke Julian.

One of the book’s memorable challenges is pushing past perceived limits through progressive self-tests — doing slightly more than comfort allows, then recovering, then extending again. Fear shrinks when faced in graded doses. Confidence grows from evidence, not affirmations alone. Kaizen is therefore both gentle and demanding: gentle because the steps are small; demanding because the steps are daily and non-negotiable.

Julian’s old model was binge intensity: enormous work sprints fueled by adrenaline, followed by collapse. Kaizen replaces binge with rhythm. Ten pages a day beats an unread library of ambitions. A short daily run beats an annual fitness panic. A nightly review beats a yearly identity crisis. Compounding favors the person who shows up while others wait to feel ready.

For modern readers, kaizen also counters comparison culture. You do not need to match someone else’s highlight reel today. You need to be measurably better than yesterday’s version of yourself in a chosen domain. That orientation reduces envy and increases agency. The sumo image reminds you that strength is built, not purchased. Even wisdom, in Sharma’s framing, is a training effect.

Lesson: Improve one small dimension of body, mind, or character every day so growth compounds instead of arriving as a failed overhaul.

Chapter 6: Live with discipline

Around the sumo wrestler is a pink wire cable — Sharma’s symbol for self-discipline and willpower. The cable looks thin at first, then proves astonishingly strong when woven from many small strands. Discipline, in this teaching, is not punishment. It is freedom purchased in advance. When you can direct your actions regardless of mood, you stop being a hostage to impulse, comfort, and social pressure.

Julian learns that willpower is trainable. Every kept promise to yourself adds a strand. Every broken promise frays the cable. This is why tiny vows matter: waking at a chosen hour, completing a short practice before checking messages, finishing a task before switching. The content of the vow can be modest; the integrity of completion is the real training stimulus. People who wait to feel disciplined before acting usually wait forever. Action creates the evidence that discipline is possible.

The monks also connect discipline to ritual. Rituals reduce negotiation. If morning contemplation happens at the same time in the same place, fewer mental resources are spent deciding whether to begin. Julian’s former life was full of intensity and low in ritual hygiene. He could work all night for a client and still lack a reliable practice for his own inner life. Discipline reverses that imbalance: protect the inner practices with the same seriousness once reserved for billable hours.

Sharma is careful to show discipline as selective, not joyless. The goal is not to control every pleasure into extinction. The goal is to govern the habits that govern you. Sleep, speech, appetite, focus, and emotional reactivity are high-leverage arenas. Master those and many secondary problems shrink. Leave them unmanaged and no motivational speech will save the week.

Discipline also has a social dimension. When you keep your word to others, trust compounds. When you keep your word to yourself, self-respect compounds. Julian’s return is impressive not because he quotes philosophy, but because his demeanor suggests a long chain of private victories. The pink cable is invisible to spectators and obvious in outcomes: steadiness under pressure, patience in conversation, follow-through without drama.

Lesson: Build willpower like a cable of small kept promises, using rituals so discipline becomes identity rather than a mood.

Chapter 7: Respect your time

The golden stopwatch symbolizes reverence for time. The sages teach that time is the most precious nonrenewable resource, yet most people spend it as if they had a spare life in reserve. Julian had been rich in money and bankrupt in hours for what mattered: health, reflection, relationships, and wonder. Respecting time means becoming deliberate about where attention goes, because attention is how time becomes a life.

Practical time mastery in the book includes planning days in advance, protecting high-value blocks for deep work and self-renewal, and reducing time thieves — unnecessary meetings, gossip, aimless scrolling, and commitments accepted only to please. Saying no becomes a spiritual practice as much as a productivity tactic. Every yes to a trivial demand is a no to the lighthouse purpose.

Julian learns to treat mornings as sacred. Early rising creates a pocket of quiet before the world’s demands arrive. In that pocket, mind training, exercise, and planning can happen without constant interruption. The point is not virtue-signaling about dawn; it is recognizing that an unmanaged morning often becomes an unmanaged self. The stopwatch also encourages urgency without panic: act while the hour is alive, but do not confuse frenzy with effectiveness.

Sharma links time respect to mortality awareness. Remembering that life is finite sharpens gratitude and prioritization. This is not meant to create dread; it is meant to end casual waste. People postpone joy, repair of relationships, and creative work as if middle age or retirement will magically supply courage. The golden stopwatch says the courage is due now.

A useful modern translation is weekly time audits. Track where hours actually went. Compare the audit to your purpose statement. The gap will be educational and sometimes embarrassing. Then redesign one block at a time. Respecting time is less about squeezing more tasks into a day and more about ensuring the day contains the few things that make the rest meaningful.

Lesson: Guard your hours like treasure — plan them, refuse trivial drains, and invest mornings in the practices that keep your purpose alive.

Chapter 8: Selflessly serve others

The roses in the fable represent kindness, compassion, and selfless service. After chapters on personal mastery, Sharma turns the camera outward. A life optimized only for self-improvement can become elegant selfishness. The monks insist that enrichment must overflow. Service is not an optional charity weekend; it is a daily orientation toward contribution.

Julian learns that giving converts knowledge into wisdom. You can meditate for years and still remain self-centered if your peace never becomes useful to anyone else. Small acts matter: listening fully, encouraging without agenda, sharing skills, forgiving sooner, helping a colleague without keeping score. The rose image suggests fragrance — influence that spreads quietly through contact. You do not need a platform to serve; you need proximity and willingness.

Service also heals the server. Julian’s old emptiness was partly the emptiness of extraction: take status, take fees, take applause. Contribution reverses the flow. Meaning increases when you experience yourself as a source rather than a consumer. This does not require abandoning healthy boundaries. Selfless in Sharma’s sense means less ego contamination, not erasing yourself. Help because it aligns with purpose, not because you are addicted to being needed.

In workplace terms, service looks like mentoring, building others’ credit, and solving problems that make the whole team stronger. In family terms, it looks like presence and practical care. In community terms, it looks like using surplus — time, money, skill — where it reduces suffering. The book’s claim is that abundance mindset and generosity reinforce each other. Scarcity mindset hoards; growth mindset shares.

The roses also challenge performative goodness. Service done for reputation reintroduces the Ferrari problem in moral costume. The test is simple: would you still do the act if nobody knew? Training that muscle keeps the virtue clean. Julian’s transformation becomes credible to John not through speeches about compassion but through the quality of attention he now offers another human being.

Lesson: Practice daily contribution without applause-seeking, so personal growth becomes generosity rather than polished self-absorption.

Chapter 9: Embrace the present

The final image is a path of diamonds: a road so filled with treasure that a traveler who rushes toward a distant destination tramples riches underfoot. The teaching is presence. Julian had lived almost entirely in anticipation — the next case, the next purchase, the next proof of worth. Even leisure was contaminated by mental rehearsal of work. He was rich in future thoughts and poor in actual moments.

Embracing the present does not mean abandoning planning. It means inhabiting the only time in which life actually occurs. Joy, craftsmanship, love, and even effective work happen now. Anxiety mostly lives in imagined futures; regret mostly lives in interpreted pasts. Presence returns the mind to the usable hour. The monks train this through mindfulness in ordinary acts: walking, eating, listening, breathing. When attention fully meets the activity, the activity becomes enough.

Sharma links presence to gratitude. Noticing what is already here — health, friendship, beauty, opportunity — interrupts the scarcity spell that drives endless striving. Julian’s Ferrari was a monument to “not enough.” Presence reveals that many of the best things were available without a courtroom victory. This realization does not kill ambition; it removes the panic from ambition. You can pursue goals without postponing your whole life until they arrive.

Practically, presence can be installed with triggers: one deep breath before answering a phone, no screens during meals, a short pause at doorways, full attention for the first minutes of a conversation. These are small gates back into the diamond path. The modern enemy is continuous partial attention — being nowhere while seeming busy everywhere. The monk’s antidote is single-task sincerity.

Presence also improves performance. A lawyer, parent, athlete, or artist who is fully in the moment notices subtle cues and responds cleanly. Julian’s new calm is not disengagement; it is engagement without friction from mental time travel. The path of diamonds is under your feet on ordinary Tuesdays. The tragedy is not that treasure is rare. The tragedy is sprinting past it.

Lesson: Stop racing toward a distant finish line and practice full attention now — the riches of life are under your feet.

Chapter 10: The garden, the lighthouse, the sumo

This chapter integrates the first half of the symbolic system so the fable can be remembered as a working model rather than a list of inspirational fragments. The garden, lighthouse, and sumo form the inner triad: mental cultivation, directional purpose, and continuous improvement. If any one is missing, the others distort. A tended mind without purpose becomes elegant aimlessness. A strong purpose without mental control becomes anxious striving. Purpose and focus without kaizen become slogans that never upgrade capacity.

Julian teaches John to walk through the images in order as a morning checklist. Garden: What am I planting in my mind today, and what weeds need removal? Lighthouse: What is the aim that makes today’s effort meaningful? Sumo: What is the one small improvement I will complete before sleep? This triad turns philosophy into a daily dashboard. It is short enough to remember and deep enough to steer behavior.

The pink cable attaches naturally to the sumo: improvement requires discipline, and discipline is trained through small acts of follow-through. Readers often try to jump to advanced practices while skipping the cable. They want Himalayan calm without keeping basic promises. Sharma’s sequencing is kinder and stricter: build reliability first. Reliability makes every later virtue portable under stress.

Seen together, these symbols also critique a common self-help failure: consuming ideas without embodiment. Julian did not merely admire the garden metaphor; he sat with the rose. He did not merely like the word purpose; he wrote and used a mission. He did not merely praise kaizen; he trained daily. Integration means the images become verbs.

For a skeptical professional like John, the triad offers a non-mystical entry point. You do not have to accept every mystical flourish of Sivana to test the model. Run thirty days of mind-tending, purpose filtering, and one daily improvement. Measure sleep quality, reactivity, and sense of meaning. Let the experiment argue with cynicism. The fable’s power is that it is memorable enough to survive a noisy calendar if you rehearse it.

Lesson: Rehearse the garden–lighthouse–sumo triad daily so mind, purpose, and incremental growth stay linked in one practice.

Chapter 11: Simplifying success theater

Selling the Ferrari is the book’s central provocation about success theater — the performance of status for an audience that cannot give you a coherent self. Julian’s possessions were not evil; they were heavy when used as identity substitutes. Sharma invites readers to simplify: remove what exists only to impress, reduce complexity that drains attention, and stop confusing luxury with a life well lived. Simplicity here is strategic clarity, not aesthetic minimalism for social media.

Success theater shows up as overwork performed for visibility, purchases made for envy management, and conversations that are networking disguised as friendship. It also shows up as the refusal to rest because rest might look like losing. Julian’s collapse was the bill for years of theater. Simplifying means rewriting the audience. If the audience is your conscience, your loved ones, and your purpose, many performances become unnecessary.

The later virtues — stopwatch, roses, diamonds — support simplification. Respecting time cuts empty obligations. Service shifts focus from being admired to being useful. Presence reduces the need to constantly announce a future self. Together they shrink the gap between appearance and reality. A simplified life still can include excellence, income, and ambition. It just stops needing every win to be displayed.

Practically, run a status audit. List expenses, commitments, and habits that exist primarily for image. Remove one. Notice the relief and the fear. The fear is useful data: it shows where identity was outsourced. Replace the removed theater with a practice from the fable — a morning ritual, a learning block, a service act, a walk without headphones. Subtraction creates space; practices fill it with substance.

Sharma’s monk is not anti-success. He is anti-hollowness. The Ferrari sale is dramatic because the audience needs a sharp symbol. Your version might be quieter: declining a vanity project, leaving a toxic prestige job, wearing ambition more lightly, or keeping wealth while refusing to let wealth narrate your worth. The point is freedom from the script that made Julian famous and sick at the same time.

Lesson: Strip status performances that do not serve purpose, and use the freed energy for practices that make success feel clean.

Chapter 12: Your monk practices this week

Philosophy becomes nutrition only when scheduled. This final chapter turns the seven virtues into a one-week install plan a busy person can actually run. Day one focuses on the garden: ten minutes of concentration practice and a quick audit of mental inputs you will reduce. Day two clarifies the lighthouse: write a one-paragraph purpose statement and list three calendar items that do not serve it. Day three begins kaizen: choose one physical practice and one learning practice small enough to complete daily.

Day four strengthens the pink cable: make two tiny vows and keep both — for example, no phone for the first fifteen minutes after waking, and a fixed shutdown time for work. Day five honors the stopwatch: plan tomorrow tonight, block one uninterrupted deep-work hour, and decline one low-value request. Day six practices roses: perform three specific acts of service or encouragement without announcing them. Day seven walks the diamond path: choose one ordinary activity — a meal, a commute, a conversation — and do it with full presence.

Throughout the week, keep a brief journal with four lines: what I practiced, what resisted, what improved, what I will repeat. The journal is not literature; it is feedback for kaizen. Expect awkwardness. Julian’s transformation looked graceful after years; your first week should look like training. Missed practices are handled with the cable principle: resume immediately rather than dramatizing failure.

At week’s end, review which virtue felt most foreign. That foreignness often marks the highest leverage gap. If presence was hardest, your life may be over-optimized for future proving. If service was hardest, growth may be too self-centered. If discipline was hardest, your vows may be too large — shrink them until integrity is easy, then scale. The monk path is progressive, not theatrical.

Carry forward only what you will still do in week two. A smaller set of living practices beats a complete set of abandoned ideals. Revisit the fable images until they are automatic: garden, lighthouse, sumo, cable, stopwatch, roses, diamonds. When stress rises, walk the symbols instead of improvising from panic. That is how a courtroom collapse becomes, over time, a composed life.

Lesson: Install the seven virtues as a one-week practice circuit, then keep only the rituals you will repeat until they become your default identity.

questions.question_text: What event forces Julian Mantle to confront his unsustainable life?
questions.option_a: Losing a major case on appeal
questions.option_b: A heart attack during a trial
questions.option_d: A public scandal about his Ferrari

questions.question_text: In the Sivana fable, what does the magnificent garden symbolize?
questions.option_c: The mind you must tend daily

questions.question_text: What does the pink wire cable around the sumo wrestler represent?
questions.option_b: Self-discipline and willpower built from small kept promises

questions.question_text: What is the teaching behind the path of diamonds?
questions.option_a: Chase distant goals at any cost
questions.option_c: Live fully in the present so you do not trample life’s riches while rushing

questions.question_text: According to the summary, what should you do after clarifying purpose?
questions.option_b: Use purpose as a filter for decisions and time
